content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Optimize CI by measuring duration, parallelizing independent work, reducing duplicate triggers, using helpful caches, and controlling matrix expansion. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Parallelizing independent jobs
items.text: List the supported combinations explicitly and use `include`/`exclude` or `max-parallel` to control expansion. Keep all required configurations covered and avoid unnecessary duplicate jobs.

items.title: Dependency caching
items.text: Cache rebuildable dependencies using a key that includes the package manager, runtime/OS as appropriate, and lockfile hash. A cache miss must not change build correctness, and secrets do not belong in caches.

items.title: Reducing unnecessary workflow triggers
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Selecting appropriate runner sizes
items.text: Choose runner labels and access boundaries that match the workload. Self-hosted machines need patching, network segmentation, secret protection, and cleanup; keep untrusted contributions away from privileged persistent runners.

items.title: Matrix design and expansion
items.text: List the supported combinations explicitly and use `include`/`exclude` or `max-parallel` to control expansion. Keep all required configurations covered and avoid unnecessary duplicate jobs.

items.title: Measuring workflow duration
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Balancing speed, cost, and confidence
items.text: Measure duration, resource/runner consumption, queue time, and failure rate before changing the pipeline. Bound retries, cancel stale work only when safe, and compare the result after one controlled change.

content_blocks.code:
jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      max-parallel: 3
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3]
    steps:
      - name: Run bounded test shard
        env:
          TEST_SHARD: ${{ matrix.shard }}
        run: echo "Run test shard $TEST_SHARD"
content_blocks.expected_output: Three shards may execute concurrently, with a 15-minute timeout per job. The command is a placeholder for a test runner that supports sharding.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Measure end-to-end runtime and queue time before and after changing parallelism. Do not infer a speedup from matrix size alone.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to ci pipeline optimization. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain ci pipeline optimization, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Build CI checks that produce repeatable evidence and protect merge quality.

content.task: Apply ci pipeline optimization to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Optimize CI by measuring duration, parallelizing independent work, reducing duplicate triggers, using helpful caches, and controlling matrix expansion.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Optimize CI by measuring duration, parallelizing independent work, reducing duplicate triggers, using helpful caches, and controlling matrix expansion. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
